text: In raw attention, one vector had to do every job at once: it was the question a token asks, the label others match against, and the content it hands over. The fix is to give every token three separate vectors, each made by its own learned matrix. Think of a library. You write a request slip describing what you need, every book carries a label on its spine, and what you finally take home is the book's content, which is not the same thing as its label.

In attention, the request slip is called the query, the label is the key, and the content is the value. Each one is made from the token's embedding by a matrix multiplication. The query matrix turns a token into a description of what it is looking for. The key matrix turns every token into a description of what it can offer. The value matrix turns every token into the information it will pass along if it is chosen. These three matrices are ordinary weights, learned by gradient descent like any other layer.

Scores now compare a query with a key. For the word it, we take its query and compute the dot product with the key of every token in the sentence. Because queries and keys come from different matrices, a token no longer scores highly with itself just because it resembles itself. The query of it can learn to describe a noun that could be tired, and the key of cat can learn to advertise exactly that, even though the words it and cat look nothing alike.

Softmax turns the scores into weights, just as before, but the weighted average is now taken over the values rather than the raw embeddings. That separation matters. The key is what gets a token chosen, and the value is what it delivers once chosen, so a token can be easy to find for one reason and contribute something quite different, the way a book's title helps you find it while its pages are what you actually read.

In matrix form, everything happens for all tokens at once. Multiply the embedding matrix X by the query weights to get Q, by the key weights to get K, and by the value weights to get V, each with one row per token. The scores are Q times the transpose of K, a square table with one row per query and one column per key. Softmax runs along each row, and the weights multiply V to give the output, again with one row per token.

It is worth walking through the shapes once, slowly, because this is where most bugs live. Suppose a sentence of five tokens with embeddings of width eight, and a query and key width of four. Then Q and K are both five by four, the transpose of K is four by five, and the score table is five by five. V is five by four as well, so the output is five rows of width four. The only rule that must hold is that queries and keys share the same width, because their dot product needs matching lengths.

Notice that nothing in these formulas says that a pronoun should look for a noun. The three matrices start out random, and training discovers which questions and which labels make the next token easier to predict. When researchers inspect trained models, they find attention patterns with recognisable jobs, such as looking back at the previous token or at an earlier copy of the current word, all learned without being written in.

Two practical details are still missing. Dot products of long vectors grow large, which pushes softmax into making overconfident choices, and a model that predicts the next token must not peek at the tokens that come after it. The next lesson deals with both, and arrives at scaled dot product attention, the exact formula used inside every transformer.
